claims.claim: Traditional respiration models require atmospheric oxygen to be transported from exchange surfaces to all body cells, implying substantial energy expenditure and speed matched to tissue metabolic demand.
Respiratory pigments are traditionally treated as passive oxygen carriers.
Melanin transforms light energy into chemical energy by dissociating the water molecule in a manner analogous to chlorophyll in plants.
Melanin can dissociate and re-form the water molecule.
Respiratory pigments can dissociate the water molecule irreversibly.
Oxygen associated with respiratory pigments is primarily due to constant water dissociation inside the pigment rather than transport from lungs to tissues.
There are four types of O2-binding pigments in animals: hemoglobin, hemocyanin, hemerythrin, and chlorocruorin.
These respiratory pigments are metalloproteins with iron or copper at the binding site.
In hemoglobin, the prosthetic group is protoheme (Fe(II)-protoporphyrin) that binds one ligand.
Hemocyanin and hemerythrin binding sites contain two metal atoms.
Chlorocruorin is a hemoprotein whose heme differs from protoheme by one substituent.
Hemocyanin and chlorocruorin are dissolved in plasma; hemerythrin is only intracellular; hemoglobin can be intra- and extracellular depending on species.
Extracellular blood pigments can reach molecular masses up to several million kDa and often have more than 100 O2-binding sites.
Oxygen does not come from the atmosphere/lungs; it comes from water dissociation inside the cell.
Dry air at 1 atm has partial pressures of about 159 mmHg O2, 594 mmHg N2, and 0.23 mmHg CO2.
When air is saturated with water vapor at 20°C and 760 mmHg, O2 partial pressure decreases to about 155.6 mmHg.
Gas solubility in water decreases as temperature increases; O2 absorption coefficients drop from about 49 to 31 to 23 ml/L at 0°C, 20°C, 40°C (at 760 mmHg).
Increasing salinity decreases O2 solubility.
At equilibrium, the partial pressure of a gas in solution equals the partial pressure of that gas in the contacting gas phase.
CO2 reacts with water to form bicarbonate/carbonate, allowing seawater to dissolve much more CO2 than distilled water before equilibrating with atmospheric CO2.
Hemoglobin-bound O2 does not contribute to the partial pressure of dissolved O2 in blood.
Oxygen diffuses about 300,000 times faster in air than in water.
Water viscosity is about 35 times that of air at 40°C and more than 100 times at 0°C.
Human resting ventilation costs about 1–2% of metabolism; fish gill ventilation at rest can exceed about 20% of metabolism.
No example of active gas transport exists in animals except carbonic anhydrase.
Oxygen diffusion in tissues is slower than in water, and diffusion alone is efficient only over short distances; circulatory convection is required in larger organisms.
Deep ocean waters have high oxygen pressure due to melanin absorbing energy (including pressure) and dissipating it by dissociating water.
Molecular homology supports common origin of life; melanin is proposed as the first spark/origin of life.
Carbonic anhydrase is near-ubiquitous, has about 6 subtypes, and catalyzes CO2↔bicarbonate rapidly in both directions.
Carbonic anhydrase turnover can reach about one million reactions per second.
Death from asphyxia is due to CO2 accumulation rather than hypoxia/anoxia.
Hemoglobin does not require oxidation of Fe(II) to Fe(III) to bind O2; methemoglobin (Fe(III)) cannot bind O2.
Structural similarity between heme and chlorophyll makes it conceivable hemoglobin can dissociate water.
Hemoglobin passively capturing/releasing O2 would require chemical energy, which is not possible because erythrocytes lack mitochondria.
Increased CO2 in blood decreases hemoglobin-mediated water dissociation, lowering PO2 primarily by reduced internal O2 generation rather than tissue O2 extraction.
Only one-third of alveolar oxygen passes into blood.
Blood oxygen solubility is about 40 ml/L or less.
CO2 transport is crucial because PCO2 above about 45 mmHg impairs energy generation/distribution via effects on water and melanin, causing dysfunction and death.
Hemoglobin water dissociation continuously produces H2 and O2; H2 diffuses out of erythrocytes, acts as energy carrier and antioxidant, and can reduce O2 to form water.
Cells do not burn glucose for energy; glucose mainly supplies carbon chains, while energy comes from H2 generated by water dissociation.
Hemoglobin oxygen saturation can remain about 96% even when inspired oxygen is as low as 7–8%.
Decreased body temperature causes a marked fall of blood oxygen tension, analogized to reduced photochemical energy conversion at low temperature in plants.
In decapod crustaceans, post-gill hemocyanin is often only 50–70% saturated even in well-aerated water; this has been interpreted as a diffusion barrier at gills.
Carbon monoxide experiments are misleading because low doses stimulate water dissociation and high doses block it.
Umbilical arterial blood oxygen saturation is about 50% lower than maternal arterial blood saturation.
Fetal energy is derived from amniotic fluid water via the same water-based energy mechanism, while maternal blood supplies building blocks.

concepts.definition: Metalloproteins that reversibly bind O2 (and sometimes other ligands) to facilitate oxygen transport or storage.
Tetrameric heme protein in vertebrate erythrocytes enabling cooperative O2 binding and transport.
Monomeric heme protein in muscle that stores O2 and facilitates intracellular O2 diffusion.
Copper-based O2-binding protein in many arthropods and mollusks, typically extracellular.
Non-heme diiron O2-binding protein in some invertebrates, typically intracellular.
Extracellular annelid respiratory pigment related to hemoglobin with modified heme, greenish when oxygenated.
Fe-protoporphyrin IX prosthetic group enabling ligand binding and redox chemistry in hemoglobin and cytochromes.
Mg-porphyrinoid pigment in photosystems; oxygenic water splitting occurs at photosystem II’s oxygen-evolving complex.
Enzyme catalyzing CO2 + H2O ⇌ HCO3− + H+, accelerating CO2 transport and acid–base regulation.

concepts.term: Henry’s law / gas partial pressure equilibrium
concepts.definition: At equilibrium, dissolved gas concentration is proportional to its partial pressure in the gas phase (with caveats for reactive gases).
Increased CO2/H+ decreases hemoglobin O2 affinity, promoting O2 unloading in tissues.
Proposed mechanism that melanin (and/or respiratory pigments) photochemically splits water to generate chemical energy and O2/H2 in animals.

logical_flow: Physical constraints -> O2 solubility and diffusion are limited in water/tissues; aquatic ventilation is energetically expensive.
Physiology baseline -> Gas exchange uses diffusion across membranes and convection via circulation; respiratory pigments bind O2 stoichiometrically.
Problem framing -> Atmospheric-to-cell O2 delivery is asserted to be too difficult under diffusion/solubility limits.
Mechanism proposal -> Melanin and respiratory pigments are asserted to dissociate water using absorbed energy (light and other forms).
Reinterpretation -> Blood/tissue O2 is asserted to originate mainly from internal water dissociation; CO2 removal becomes the primary driver of ventilation/circulation.
Enzymatic emphasis -> Carbonic anhydrase ubiquity and high turnover are taken to indicate CO2 management dominance.
Extensions -> Exercise, deep-sea oxygenation, erythrocyte energetics, and fetal metabolism are re-explained via pigment-driven water dissociation and H2-based energy carriage.
Conclusion -> Revising respiration around melanin/pigment water dissociation is asserted to resolve outstanding physiological 'mysteries'.
